how-it-works.alt: How unroad works: you talk to your agent with /ur-learn; the agent runs the engine, ur; the engine serves one step; you and the agent do the work; ur done checks the step's gates in code. A pass serves the next step, a fail keeps the same step and gives the reason. Progress is saved in ~/.unroad, in state.json and a hash-chained log.jsonl, and the roadmap app reads the same state.

topic-anatomy.alt: The five steps of every topic, in order, each checked in code before the next: lesson (the lesson was shown), quiz (every answer is correct), lab (the lab checks pass on disk), reflection (at least 30 characters in your own words) and review (every checklist item confirmed).

curriculum-map.alt: The curriculum: ten stages in order, 01 Foundations (4 topics); 02 Prompting and context (4 topics); 03 Agent setup (6 topics); 04 Specs before code (6 topics); 05 BMAD Method (5 topics); 06 The build loop (5 topics); 07 Quality (4 topics); 08 Security (3 topics); 09 Harness and delivery (4 topics); 10 Leading the change (8 topics). 49 topics in all, each at one of three levels: foundation, practitioner or expert; the map shows how many topics of each level every stage has.

stage-01.alt: Stage 01, Foundations: How LLMs and agents actually work, and the habits that separate engineering from guessing. 4 topics.

stage-02.alt: Stage 02, Prompting and context: Give the agent the smallest set of high-signal information that gets the right result. 4 topics.

stage-03.alt: Stage 03, Agent setup: A configured, safe and repeatable environment beats a default one with everything switched on. 6 topics.

stage-04.alt: Stage 04, Specs before code: A spec is the contract between you and the agent: what, for whom, by which rules, and how you know it is done. 6 topics.

stage-05.alt: Stage 05, BMAD Method: An open agile framework where agent roles run analysis, planning, solutioning and implementation. 5 topics.

stage-06.alt: Stage 06, The build loop: Explore, plan, implement, verify. Small steps, tests as the target, clear limits. 5 topics.

stage-07.alt: Stage 07, Quality: Tests, review and evals are the sensors that let you trust agent output. 4 topics.

stage-08.alt: Stage 08, Security: An agent with access to code, secrets and the network is a new attack surface. 3 topics.

stage-09.alt: Stage 09, Harness and delivery: Everything around the agent: guides, sensors, CI, commits, releases and parallel work. 4 topics.

stage-10.alt: Stage 10, Leading the change: Bring what works to your team: a story with evidence, a pilot, agreements, coaching, policy and metrics. 8 topics.

what-is-an-agent.alt: The agent loop: you give a task; the model reads the context and proposes a tool call (decision); the harness checks permissions, allow, ask or deny, and runs the tool (execution); the result is appended to the context (observation); the model decides again, until it gives a final answer. Permissions, sandboxes and hooks act in the harness, between the decision and the execution.

how-llms-work.alt: The context window is a fixed budget. Every request carries the system prompt, tool definitions and instruction files, which are always loaded and paid for on every turn, then the conversation, every file read and command output, and your newest message, which accumulate. When the window fills, the harness compacts it and details are lost. Attention is spread across everything in the window, so a rule that stood out in a fresh session is one line among thousands later.

context-engineering.alt: Two ways to give an agent context. Pasting everything, five source files and a 2,400-line test log, fills the window with noise, and the agent fixes the first suspicious thing it notices instead of the real bug. Just-in-time retrieval gives a few pointers, a function, a doc section and a reproduce command, and the agent loads only what it needs, finding the bug with a fraction of the context.

instruction-files.alt: One instruction file, many tools. AGENTS.md at the repository root is the source of truth: Codex reads it from the root down to the current directory, Cursor reads it in the root and subdirectories, and Copilot reads it with the nearest file taking precedence. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, which imports the shared file with @AGENTS.md and adds Claude-only lines.

long-sessions.alt: Long sessions and memory. During a session the context fills with file contents and test output; compaction replaces it with a summary that keeps the gist and loses detail. At the end of a session the agent updates progress.md and decisions.md on disk and you commit; a fresh session reads those files and git log, summarises where things stand and runs the tests before it continues.

permissions.alt: Permissions and sandboxing. Every tool call is checked against three rule lists, deny first, then ask, then allow; the first match decides. Deny blocks the call, for example Read(./.env); ask prompts you, for example Bash(git push *); allow runs without asking, for example Bash(npm test *). Shell commands that run then stay inside an operating-system sandbox: writes only in the working directory, network only to allowed domains, and reads of paths such as ~/.ssh denied. Hooks, MCP servers and the built-in file and web tools run outside the sandbox and follow the permission rules.

hooks.alt: How a hook works. An event fires, for example PreToolUse before a Bash call; the matching hook script receives the call as JSON on stdin and answers with an exit code. Exit 0 lets the call continue, and the normal permission checks still apply. Exit 2 blocks it, and the message on stderr goes back to the agent, which reads the reason and adjusts.

skills.alt: Progressive disclosure in Agent Skills. The name and description of every skill are always loaded. When a task matches a description, the body of that skill's SKILL.md loads, ideally under about 500 lines. Files in scripts, references and assets load only when the instructions point to them and the task needs them; a script's output enters the context, not its source.

spec-first.alt: From idea to agent: an idea, a PR/FAQ that tests the customer value, a one-page spec with rules and non-goals, numbered acceptance criteria, small vertical slices, and a readiness gate before an agent builds against the criteria. A gap found at the gate goes back into the spec. Deciding before code costs a sentence; deciding after costs a rewrite.

bmad-overview.alt: The four BMAD phases. Analysis, optional: brainstorming, forge idea, product brief and PRFAQ skills, writing brief.md, research.md and a PRFAQ. Planning: bmad-prd, bmad-ux and bmad-spec, writing prd.md, DESIGN.md, EXPERIENCE.md and SPEC.md. Solutioning: bmad-architecture, bmad-create-epics-and-stories and bmad-sprint-planning, writing ARCHITECTURE-SPINE.md, epics.md and sprint-status.yaml. Implementation: bmad-build, bmad-code-review, bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests and bmad-retrospective, producing a spec per story, code and commits, and a retrospective. A small change goes straight to bmad-build, an epic-sized change runs bmad-spec and then one build per story, a multi-epic product uses the full path.

explore-plan-implement-verify.alt: The four-phase build loop and where each mistake is cheapest to catch. Explore reads without writing and catches wrong assumptions about the code for the cost of a sentence. Plan proposes steps and checks you can edit and catches a wrong approach for the cost of an edited line. Implement makes one step and one check at a time, so a broken step costs a revert, then loops back for the next step. Verify runs the commands and shows their output, so a claim without evidence is fixed before review, not after merge.

test-first.alt: Test-first with an agent, in four turns. The agent writes a test list and you review the behaviour; it writes the test code and you check that the tests say what the list says; the red run must fail on its assertions, not on an import error, and then the tests are committed; the agent implements with the tests frozen until they pass, changing code only. An empty git diff on the tests folder proves the target did not move.

guides-and-sensors.alt: Guides and sensors around an agent. Guides act before the agent does, to raise the odds of a good first attempt: computational ones such as generators, codemods and templates, inferential ones such as AGENTS.md, specs and skills. Sensors act after, so the agent notices a bad attempt and fixes it: computational ones such as tests, the type checker and the linter, inferential ones such as AI review and human review. Sensors work best close to the agent: a hook in seconds, pre-commit in minutes, CI after the push.

prompt-injection.alt: The lethal trifecta for prompt injection: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. With all three, injected text can make the agent read your data and send it out. Break any one leg and the attack fails: remove the way out with a sandbox and a narrow network allowlist, remove private data with narrow tokens and deny rules, or remove untrusted content by splitting sessions so a person reads the summary in between.

parallel-agents.alt: Parallel agents with git worktrees. Two branches leave main, each in its own worktree directory with its own agent, sharing one .git store. Merge them back one at a time: merge task-a and run the tests on main; rebase task-b onto the new main and run its tests in the worktree; merge task-b and run the tests again.

evals.alt: Building evals for an AI feature: collect real traces; do error analysis by reading them and noting pass or fail and the first thing that went wrong; group the notes into a small, counted failure taxonomy; fix the obvious failures directly; write code checks first and a validated LLM judge, one binary judge per failure mode, where no rule can decide; run them in CI whenever the prompt, model, retrieval or tools change, and read fresh traces again from time to time.

run-a-pilot.alt: Running a pilot: take a baseline of the same measures for six to eight weeks before, and commit the success criteria before day one; run a two to four week pilot with one team and one kind of work, inside guardrails for what agents may and may not do, human review on every pull request and no customer data in prompts; hold the review and apply the criteria as written: scale, adjust and run another timebox, or stop.
